 ‘Dark money’ groups are spending millions opposing Amendment 87, which proposes graduated income tax in Colorado
 Dozens of nonprofits and hundreds of individual Coloradans have donated to support Amendment 87, while a handful of large donations fuel its opposition
 News News | Oct 18, 2026 
 Ryan Spencer Follow 
 rspencer@steamboatpilot.com

 Millions of dollars are flowing into November’s election in an effort to sway Coloradans’ vote on two ballot measures related to the state’s income tax system .
 Supporters of Amendment 87, which would replace the state’s flat income tax with a graduated system, had disclosed around $1 million in spending as of the Oct. 6 filing deadline with the Colorado Secretary of State’s Office. The Amendment 87 campaign received small donations between $5 and $500 from about 300 individual Colorado residents, as well as contributions from dozens of nonprofits with local and state ties, according to the filings.
 The opposition to Amendment 87 had disclosed more than $3.6 million in spending amid an influx by the deadline. While filings show a couple dozen individual donations from Coloradans, the vast majority of this money came via large donations from groups that don’t disclose their donors.
 “Lots of people are very intent on making sure that taxes for billionaires and millionaires and Colorado’s biggest corporations stay locked in at the same rate that you and I pay, which I think is pretty outrageous,” said Ian Silverii, with the Protect Colorado’s Future Coalition, which petitioned for Amendment 87 to be on the ballot.
 Amendment 87 would increase the tax rate for incomes above $500,000, and lower taxes for anyone making less than that, raising an additional $2.7 billion for the state government to spend on healthcare, education and childcare.

 Silverii described the millions of dollars opposing Amendment 87 as “dark money” because the vast majority of it comes from conservative political advocacy groups registered as 501(c)(4) organizations, which don’t have to disclose their donors.
 More information on Amendment 87 can be found on page 33 of the 2026 State Ballot Information Booklet. Ryan Spencer/Post Independent 
 Advance Colorado — a nonprofit founded in 2020 by former Republican Gov. Bill Owen — is leading the opposition to Amendment 87. It does not disclose its donors, but reporting from news outlets including the Denver Post have revealed major support from billionaire Phil Anschutz .
 The conservative group is also connected to roughly half of the 14 ballot measures before voters this election cycle, including Proposition 136 — which is a direct countermeasure to Amendment 87.
 Prop 136 proposes to maintain Colorado’s flat tax rate of 4.4%. On its own, Prop 136 has the same result of maintaining the existing flat tax rate in the Colorado Taxpayer Bill of Rights, whether it passes or fails. But, if both Prop 136 and Amendment 87 pass with a 50% majority vote, it could create legal questions that would have to be answered by a court, according to the official voter information packet.
 Kristi Burton Brown, Advance Colorado’s executive vice president, said that voters’ top concern should be what the policy of a ballot measure does — not which group funds the proposed policy.
 Burton Brown also accused the supporters of Amendment 87 of accepting large donations and said groups like the Bell Policy Center are also “dark money” groups that aren’t required to disclose their donors. 
 When asked who funds Advance Colorado, she said it would be “unethical” to disclose donors without their permission but added there have been “thousands” of donations in opposition to the graduated income tax measure.
 “We comply with all the laws, all the regulations. Everything we do is fully above board,” she said. “I think that’s just a distraction tactic that the other side uses when they don’t want to actually talk about policy.”
 But Silverii said comparing the Bell Policy Center to the “dark money” funding Advance Colorado is “insulting to anybody with a brain,” as the organization is Colorado-based and has been more transparent about its donors. He added that Coloradans should know who is behind the barrage of political advertising they face each election season and that the state’s campaign finance system “is badly in need of updates and reforms.”
 Describing the support for Amendment 87 as a “people-powered, volunteer-driven campaign,” Silverii said the monied interests opposed to the ballot measure are spending millions on deceptive ads. Rather than engage in a vigorous policy debate, he said Advance Colorado and its related entities have called Amendment 87 a tax hike — even though it would reduce taxes for the vast majority of Coloradans — and focused on untrue claims that it would impact social security beneficiaries and veterans.
 “The main difference is that their money is being hidden by out-of-state dark money groups, so we can’t tell where it’s coming from,” Silverii said. “Our money is coming from Colorado and Coloradans.”
 More information about Proposition 136 can be found on page 62 of the 2026 State Ballot Information Booklet. Ryan Spencer/Post Independent 
 Who is funding the opposition to Amendment 87? 
 Filings with the Secretary of State’s Office show a sudden influx of millions of dollars between mid-September and early October — with ballots mailed to voters starting Oct. 2 — to groups registered as opposing Amendment 87. The vast majority of the money is coming from a few large donations made by 501(c)(4)s, cloaking who exactly is behind them.
 A Brighter Colorado — an issue committee that shares an agent with Advance Colorado and is registered as opposing Amendment 87 and Prop NN — had raised and spent about $2.6 million as of its Oct. 6 report.
 According to the Secretary of State’s Office, Brighter Colorado disclosed $2 million in donations from A Common Sense America , a conservative advocacy group with a registered address in Virginia, and a $500,000 contribution from GOPAC Election Fund , a national Republican political action committee also based in Virginia. The filings also show about a dozen individual donations between $25 and $500, as well as a handful of larger donations between $5,000 and $25,000 from Colorado residents.
 Brighter Colorado has spent most of the money it has raised with a Colorado Springs-based canvassing business for advertising and consulting services, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
 Don’t Price Us Out — another issue committee registered as opposed to Amendment 87 — is also associated with Advance Colorado through registered agents and the West Group , a law and policy center that represents “large corporations, private companies and nonprofit organizations.”
 Filings show Don’t Price Us Out received just two donations by the Oct. 6 deadline: A $760,000 contribution from American Prosperity Coalition, a 501(c)(4) with a registered address in Texas, and a $300,000 contribution from Ready Colorado, a 501(c)(4) registered in Lakewood. That money has gone almost entirely to advertising, including $824,000 to a Denver-based digital media company.
 Americans for Prosperity, a 501(c)(4) founded by billionaire Robert Koch, has also registered an issue committee in opposition to Amendment 87. Filings show the Virginia-based group has contributed more than $265,000 to oppose the ballot measure, nearly all of that spent on doorhangers, digital ads and canvassing.
 Multi-million dollar homes sit on a hill above a mobile home park in Edwards. Chris Dillmann/Vail Daily 
 Who is supporting Amendment 87? 
 Protect Colorado’s Future — the group supporting Amendment 87 — has raised about $1.2 million, spent about $946,000 and received about $400,000 in nonmonetary donations over the course of several months, according to the latest filings.
 Filings show Amendment 87 received the majority of its financial support from local and state nonprofits like Great Education Colorado, Colorado Consumer Health Initiative, Colorado Cross Disability Coalition, Hunger Free Colorado, Colorado Statewide Parent Coalition and about a dozen others.
 Merle Chambers, a retired lawyer and philanthropist who lives in Denver, is the single largest contributor to Amendment 87, having donated $250,000 to support the ballot measure and $100,000 to oppose Prop 136.
 The Bell Policy Center — a Denver-based nonprofit focused on research, policy analysis and public education founded by Chambers in 2000 — has also contributed about $135,000 to support Amendment 87.
 “These are community-based organizations doing work in this community that are moving money into this campaign because they recognize the importance of passing this measure to protect the future of Colorado,” said Bell Policy Center President Chris deGruy Kennedy.
 Kennedy said that many groups that have supported Amendment 87, including the Bell Policy Center, are 501(c)(3) nonprofits and face far stricter limits from the Internal Revenue Service on election spending than 501(c)(4)s. He said that, while not required to disclose donors, the community-facing nonprofits supporting Amendment 87 are transparent about where the funding is coming from and are dealing with significantly smaller amounts of money than the opposition.
 Protect Colorado’s Future has documented its spending for months. In the first six months of the year, it spent about $75,0000 on everything from petition packets, teleconference services, campaign consulting, gas mileage and more.
 Over the past three months, the campaign has disclosed about $1.18 million in spending on field organizing, campaign management and advertising. That includes a $200,000 ad purchase late last month and hundreds of thousands of dollars in “non-monetary expenses,” usually detailed as campaign consulting services.
 By the nature of the question Amendment 87 is asking, Kennedy said the Protect Colorado’s Future Coalition doesn’t expect to get a ton of financial support from the billionaires and multi-millionaires it proposes to raise taxes on. 
 Protect Colorado’s Future Coalition has also received about 300 donations between $5 and $500 from individual state residents, totalling about $27,000, according to filings. Kennedy said the campaign appreciates every donation, but noted how quickly a million-dollar donation on the other side, likely from a large corporation or a billionaire, can outweigh hundreds of small donations. 
 “At the end of the day,” he said, “we expect to be outspent at least four-to-one on the campaign.”
